summary: Probability and statistics has a small toolkit that the questions reuse: conditional probability with total probability and Bayes, linearity of expectation, the mean and variance of the standard distributions, and the descriptive statistics of a data set. Most questions are short calculations, so the marks go to whoever sets up the sample space and events cleanly, then picks the right identity without mixing up independence and mutual exclusion.
highYield: A two-stage Bayes question (urns, machines, diagnostic tests): build the total-probability denominator over every branch, then divide out the branch asked for.
Mean and variance of binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, exponential and normal as direct 1-mark questions, including Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
Linearity of expectation with indicator variables for counts such as fixed points of a permutation, which needs no independence.
Finding the constant k that makes a PDF integrate to 1, then a probability, mean or median from it.
Mean, median, mode and standard deviation of a small data set, with the population (÷n) versus sample (÷(n − 1)) convention stated in the question.

topics.title: Sample spaces, events and counting probability
points: A sample space S is the set of all outcomes of an experiment, an event is a subset of S, and a probability assigns each event a value in [0, 1] with P(S) = 1 and additivity over disjoint events.
Complement and inclusion–exclusion follow from the axioms: P(A′) = 1 − P(A) and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for three events add back the triple intersection after subtracting all pairs.
With equally likely outcomes, P(E) = |E| / |S|, so the problem becomes counting: two dice give 36 ordered outcomes and 6 of them sum to 7, so P = 1/6.
For “at least one” use the complement: P(at least one head in 3 tosses) = 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8, and P(some shared birthday among 5 people) = 1 − (365·364·363·362·361)/365⁵ ≈ 0.0271.
Drawing without replacement is hypergeometric: choosing k red from a urn of R red and B blue in n draws has probability C(R, k)·C(B, n − k)/C(R + B, n).

lesson.why: Most probability questions reduce to counting outcomes correctly, and the complement rule turns every at-least-one question into a short calculation.
lesson.intro: An experiment is anything with an uncertain result, such as rolling two dice. The sample space is the list of every possible result. An event is any chosen group of those results, for example the results where the dice add to 7. When all results are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of results in it divided by the number of results in the sample space.

analogy.text: Probability is the share of a pizza: the sample space is the whole pizza and an event is the slices you pick.
analogy.breaksWhen: The slices must be equal in size; if outcomes are not equally likely, counting them gives the wrong share.

definitions.meaning: The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.
A subset of the sample space, one or more outcomes grouped by a condition.
The event that A does not happen, written $A'$, with $P(A') = 1 - P(A)$.

principle.text: With equally likely outcomes, $P(E)$ is the count of outcomes in $E$ over the count in the sample space. For any two events, the overlap must be removed once so it is not counted twice.

lesson.limits: Counting works only when every outcome in the chosen sample space is equally likely. The sum of two dice is not: a sum of 7 has six ways and a sum of 2 has one, so count ordered pairs, not sums.

example.problem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one shows a 6?
steps: The sample space has $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered pairs.
Count the complement, no 6 on either die: $5 \times 5 = 25$ pairs.

misconceptions: Treating the sum of two dice as the outcome: sums are not equally likely, so counting 11 possible sums and dividing is wrong.
Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ for an either-or event and forgetting to subtract the overlap, which can push the answer above 1.

recall.q: When is the formula $|E|/|S|$ valid?
recall.a: Only when every outcome in the sample space is equally likely.

recall.q: Which rule is fastest for an at-least-one event?
recall.a: The complement rule: compute the probability that none happens and subtract it from 1.

recall.q: How do you find $P(A \cup B)$?
recall.a: Add $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, then subtract $P(A \cap B)$ because the overlap was counted twice.

practice.stem: A number is chosen uniformly at random from $\{1, 2, \ldots, 30\}$. What is the probability that it is divisible by 2 or by 3?
practice.explanation: There are 15 multiples of 2, 10 multiples of 3 and 5 multiples of 6, so the count is $15 + 10 - 5 = 20$ and the probability is $20/30 = 2/3$. Adding 15 and 10 without removing the 5 overlap would give $25/30$. The choice 1/2 tempts because it counts only the multiples of 2.

lesson.summary: List the equally likely outcomes, count the event, divide; use the complement for at-least-one and subtract the overlap for either-or.

topics.title: Conditional probability and the multiplication rule
points: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) for P(B) > 0: conditioning on B shrinks the sample space to B and renormalises.
The multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)·P(B) = P(B | A)·P(A) chains to P(A₁ ∩ … ∩ Aₙ) = P(A₁)·P(A₂ | A₁)·P(A₃ | A₁ ∩ A₂)…, which is how sequential draws without replacement are computed.
When the union is given instead of the intersection, recover the intersection first: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, P(A ∪ B) = 0.8 give P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 and P(A | B) = 0.6.
P(· | B) is itself a probability measure, so complements and inclusion–exclusion hold inside it: P(A′ | B) = 1 − P(A | B).

lesson.why: Sequential draws, given-that questions and Bayes problems all rest on the definition of conditional probability.
lesson.intro: Sometimes you learn that something has already happened and must update the odds. The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is the chance of $A$ when you only consider the cases where $B$ happened. Knowing $B$ throws away every outcome outside $B$, and the remaining outcomes are rescaled so they add up to 1 again.

principle.text: The conditional probability is the overlap divided by the probability of the condition. Rearranged, it gives the multiplication rule for building up joint events step by step.
principle.tex: P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(A\cap B)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)

lesson.limits: The definition needs $P(B) > 0$. The two directions are different quantities: $P(A \mid B)$ is usually not equal to $P(B \mid A)$.

example.problem: An urn holds 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
steps: The first draw is red with probability $4/10$.
Given that, 3 red balls remain among 9, so the second is red with probability $3/9$.

misconceptions: Using $4/10$ again for the second draw: without replacement the urn has changed, so the second factor must be conditional.
Reading $P(A \mid B)$ as $P(B \mid A)$; the probability that a spade is a card of rank ace differs from the probability that an ace is a spade.

recall.q: What is the formula for $P(A \mid B)$?
recall.a: $P(A \cap B)/P(B)$, defined when $P(B) > 0$.

recall.q: How do you get $P(A \cap B)$ when you are given $P(A \cup B)$?
recall.a: Use $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$.

practice.stem: For two events, $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.6$. Find $P(A \mid B)$.
practice.explanation: The overlap is $0.5 + 0.4 - 0.6 = 0.3$, so $P(A \mid B) = 0.3/0.4 = 0.75$. Dividing by $P(A)$ instead gives 0.6, which is $P(B \mid A)$ and is the tempting wrong answer.

lesson.summary: Conditioning restricts to $B$ and rescales: divide the overlap by $P(B)$, and multiply conditional factors to chain draws without replacement.

topics.title: Independence versus mutual exclusion
points: A and B are independent iff P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) when P(B) > 0; mutually exclusive means A ∩ B = ∅, so P(A ∩ B) = 0.
Two events with positive probabilities cannot be both independent and mutually exclusive, because then P(A)·P(B) > 0 = P(A ∩ B).
If A and B are independent, so are A and B′, A′ and B, and A′ and B′.

Three events are mutually independent only if every pair factorises and P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)P(B)P(C); pairwise independence alone is not enough (two fair coin tosses with C = “both tosses agree” is the standard counterexample).

lesson.why: Independence is what allows probabilities to be multiplied, and exam options often test whether you can tell it apart from mutual exclusion.
lesson.intro: Two events are independent when learning that one happened does not change the chance of the other. Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot happen together. These sound similar but are close to opposites: if two possible events cannot occur together, then knowing one occurred tells you the other did not.

definitions.meaning: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
$A \cap B$ is empty, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$.

principle.text: Test independence by checking whether the joint probability equals the product of the separate probabilities. Never decide it by intuition about cause.

lesson.limits: Three events are mutually independent only if every pair factorises and the triple product also holds; pairwise independence alone is not enough. Independence also depends on the probability model, not on whether events seem physically unrelated.

example.problem: Two fair dice are rolled. Let $A$ be the event that the first die is even and $B$ the event that the sum is 7. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?
steps: The pairs in both events are (2,5), (4,3) and (6,1), so $P(A \cap B) = 3/36 = 1/12$.

misconceptions: Believing mutually exclusive events are independent: with positive probabilities, $P(A \cap B) = 0$ but $P(A)P(B) > 0$, so they are dependent.
Assuming pairwise independence of three events means they are mutually independent; the triple product must be checked too.

recall.q: What is the product test for independence?
recall.a: $A$ and $B$ are independent exactly when $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$.

recall.q: Can two events with positive probability be both independent and mutually exclusive?
recall.a: No, because independence needs a positive overlap probability while exclusivity makes it zero.

practice.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ have $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$. Which statement is true?
options: $A$ and $B$ are neither independent nor exclusive
practice.explanation: The overlap is $0.4 + 0.5 - 0.7 = 0.2$, which equals $0.4 \times 0.5$, so the events are independent. They are not exclusive because the overlap is not zero. The option claiming exclusivity tempts if you see the union is below 1; the last option tempts if you skip the product check.

lesson.summary: Independent means the joint probability is the product; exclusive means the joint probability is zero; positive-probability events cannot be both.

topics.title: Total probability and Bayes' theorem
points: If B₁, …, Bₖ partition S, then P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)·P(Bᵢ): split the event over the branch that generated it.
Bayes reverses the conditioning: P(Bᵢ | A) = P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(A | Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ), the share of branch i in the total probability of A.
Urn template: box 1 has 3 red and 2 blue, box 2 has 2 red and 3 blue, a box is chosen at random and a red ball drawn; P(box 1 | red) = (3/10)/(5/10) = 3/5.
Machine template: shares 50%, 30%, 20% with defect rates 1%, 2%, 3% give an overall defect rate of 0.017, and a defective item came from the third machine with probability 0.006/0.017 ≈ 0.353.
Test template: with prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99% and false-positive rate 1%, P(disease | positive) = 0.0099/0.0198 = 0.5, far below the 99% intuition because healthy people dominate the population.

lesson.why: Defect, test and urn questions are all two-stage experiments, and this topic gives the standard method to solve any of them.
lesson.intro: Often a result can arise from several different causes, and you know how likely each cause is and how likely each produces the result. Total probability adds up the contributions of every cause to get the chance of the result. Bayes' theorem then runs the question backwards: given that the result occurred, how likely was each cause?

analogy.text: Think of a detective: the causes are suspects, the result is the evidence, and Bayes' theorem shares out the blame in proportion to how much of the evidence each suspect explains.
analogy.breaksWhen: The shares are only valid if the suspects cover every possibility and exclude each other; a missing or overlapping cause breaks the sum.

definitions.meaning: A set of events that do not overlap and together cover the whole sample space.
The prior is the probability of a cause before the result is seen; the posterior is its probability after.

principle.text: Total probability weights each branch by its prior. Bayes divides one branch's contribution by that total.
principle.tex: P(A)=\sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i),\qquad P(B_j\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_j)P(B_j)}{\sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i)}

lesson.limits: The causes must form a partition: exclusive and exhaustive. If they overlap or leave gaps, the denominator is wrong and the posteriors will not add to 1.

example.problem: Machine $A$ makes 60% of items with a 2% defect rate; machine $B$ makes 40% with a 5% defect rate. An item is found defective. What is the probability it came from $A$?
example.result: The item came from $A$ with probability 0.375, even though $A$ makes most of the items.

misconceptions: Answering with the prior (0.6): the evidence of a defect shifts belief toward the machine with the higher defect rate.
Forgetting the denominator and reporting the branch product alone, which is not a probability given the result.

recall.q: What does total probability compute?
recall.a: The chance of a result as the sum over all causes of the cause probability times the result probability given that cause.

recall.q: What must hold for the causes in Bayes' theorem?
recall.a: They must form a partition: mutually exclusive and covering every case.

practice.stem: 25% of mail is spam. A given word appears in 60% of spam and in 10% of non-spam. A message contains the word. Find the probability it is spam, rounded to two decimal places.
practice.explanation: Spam with the word: $0.25 \times 0.6 = 0.15$. Non-spam with the word: $0.75 \times 0.1 = 0.075$. The posterior is $0.15/0.225 = 2/3 \approx 0.67$. The value 0.6 tempts because it is the word rate within spam, which is the reverse conditional.

lesson.summary: Weight each cause by its prior to get the total, then divide one cause's share by that total to reverse the conditioning.

topics.title: Random variables, PMF, PDF and CDF
points: A random variable maps each outcome to a real number; it is discrete when it takes countably many values and continuous when it has a density.
A PMF satisfies p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1; a PDF satisfies f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over the real line, and f(x) itself may exceed 1.
The CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is non-decreasing and right-continuous with F(−∞) = 0 and F(∞) = 1; for a continuous X, f = F′ and P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).
For a continuous X, P(X = a) = 0, so ≤ and < give the same probabilities; for a discrete X they differ by the mass at the endpoint.
A typical question fixes a constant: f(x) = kx² on [0, 3] needs k·9 = 1, so k = 1/9, P(X ≤ 1) = 1/27 and E[X] = 9/4.

lesson.why: Every distribution question starts by turning a density or a table into probabilities, and the normalising constant is the first step in density questions.
lesson.intro: A random variable is a number that depends on the outcome of an experiment, such as the sum shown by two dice. If it can take only separate values, a table of probabilities describes it. If it can take any value in a range, no single value has positive probability and a density curve is used instead: the probability of a range is the area under the curve over that range.

definitions.meaning: For a discrete variable, $p(x) = P(X = x)$; the values add up to 1.
For a continuous variable, a density $f(x) \ge 0$ whose total area is 1; probabilities are areas.
$F(x) = P(X \le x)$, which never decreases and runs from 0 to 1.

principle.text: Total probability must be 1, which fixes any unknown constant. A range probability is an area, or a difference of the CDF.

lesson.limits: A density can exceed 1 because it is not a probability; only areas are. For a continuous variable $P(X = a) = 0$, so endpoints do not matter, but for a discrete variable they do.

example.problem: A variable has density $f(x) = kx$ on $[0, 2]$ and 0 elsewhere. Find $k$ and $P(X \le 1)$.
steps: The area must be 1: $\int_0^2 kx\,dx = k \cdot 2 = 1$, so $k = 1/2$.

misconceptions: Thinking a density value above 1 is an error; only the area has to be at most 1.
Treating $P(X = a)$ as the height $f(a)$ for a continuous variable; the probability of a single point is 0.

recall.q: How do you find the constant in a density?
recall.a: Set the integral of the density over the range where it is nonzero equal to 1 and solve.

recall.q: How does the CDF give $P(a \le X \le b)$ for a continuous variable?
recall.a: It is $F(b) - F(a)$.

practice.stem: A variable has density $f(x) = kx^3$ on $[0, 2]$ and 0 elsewhere. Find $P(X \le 1)$.
practice.explanation: Normalising: $k \cdot 2^4/4 = 4k = 1$, so $k = 1/4$. Then $P(X \le 1) = \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot\tfrac{1}{4} = 1/16 = 0.0625$. The value 0.5 tempts if you take the interval [0,1] as half of [0,2], but the density is not uniform.

lesson.summary: Fix the constant by making the total 1, then read probabilities as sums for a PMF or areas for a PDF.

topics.title: Expectation, variance and linearity
points: E[X] = Σ x·p(x) for discrete X and ∫ x·f(x) dx for continuous X; for any function g, E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x) or ∫ g(x)f(x) dx without first finding the distribution of g(X).
Linearity E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c holds for any random variables, dependent or not.
Indicator trick: write a count as a sum of 0/1 indicators, so E[count] = Σ P(event i); a random permutation of n items has n·(1/n) = 1 expected fixed point for every n.
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])² and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X); for three fair coin tosses Var = 0.75 and E[X²] = 0.75 + 1.5² = 3.
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y), which reduces to Var(X) + Var(Y) only when X and Y are uncorrelated, in particular when independent; Var(X − Y) also adds the variances.

lesson.why: Mean and variance appear in nearly every distribution question, and linearity of expectation solves counting problems that look hard.
lesson.intro: The expected value is the long-run average of a random variable: each value weighted by its probability. The variance measures how far values typically stray from that average, by averaging the squared distance. Squaring keeps below-average and above-average deviations from cancelling out.

definitions.meaning: $E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c$, true even when $X$ and $Y$ are dependent.
If $X \le Y$ in every outcome, then $E[X] \le E[Y]$; expectation preserves inequalities.
A variable that is 1 when an event happens and 0 otherwise, so its expectation is the event's probability.

principle.text: Expectation is a probability-weighted sum, and variance is the mean square minus the square of the mean. Adding a constant leaves variance unchanged and scaling multiplies it by the square.

lesson.limits: Variances add, $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$, only when the covariance is zero, for example for independent variables. In general $E[X^2]$ is not $(E[X])^2$ and $E[XY]$ is not $E[X]E[Y]$.

example.problem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find the expected value and the variance of the result.

misconceptions: Computing variance as $E[X^2]$ without subtracting the squared mean, or as $(E[X])^2$; the correct form is the difference.
Believing $\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a\,\mathrm{Var}(X) + b$; the constant disappears and the multiplier is squared.

recall.q: State the shortcut formula for variance.
recall.a: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$.

recall.q: Does linearity of expectation need independence?
recall.a: No, it holds for any random variables, dependent or not.

recall.q: If $X \le Y$ in every outcome, what follows for the means?
recall.a: $E[X] \le E[Y]$, because expectation preserves inequalities.

recall.q: How does variance change under $aX + b$?
recall.a: It becomes $a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)$; the shift $b$ has no effect.

practice.stem: $X$ takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. Find $\mathrm{Var}(3X - 2)$.
practice.explanation: $E[X] = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1$ and $E[X^2] = 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(3X - 2) = 9 \times 0.49 = 4.41$. The value 1.47 tempts if you multiply by 3 instead of squaring it, and subtracting 2 changes nothing.

lesson.summary: Weight values by probability for the mean, subtract the squared mean from the mean square for variance, and square any multiplier.

topics.title: Bernoulli trials: Bernoulli, binomial and geometric
points: Bernoulli(p) is one trial with P(X = 1) = p: mean p and variance p(1 − p), which peaks at 1/4 when p = 1/2.
Binomial B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials with the same p: P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, mean np and variance np(1 − p); B(10, 0.3) gives P(X = 2) ≈ 0.2335, mean 3 and variance 2.1.
Geometric(p) counts trials up to and including the first success: P(X = k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p, mean 1/p and variance (1 − p)/p²; the first head on the third toss has probability 1/8.
The geometric distribution is the discrete memoryless one: P(X > m + n | X > m) = P(X > n), so after 3 failed tosses the expected total is 3 + 1/p.
Check the convention: some texts count failures before the first success, which shifts the mean to (1 − p)/p and leaves the variance unchanged.

lesson.why: Counting successes in repeated independent trials, or waiting for the first one, is the most common setup in GATE probability numericals.
lesson.intro: A trial is an experiment with two outcomes, success with probability $p$ and failure with probability $1-p$. If you repeat it $n$ times and every trial is independent with the same $p$, the number of successes is binomial. If you instead keep repeating until the first success, the number of trials needed is geometric. Both come from the same idea: independent trials multiply their probabilities.

definitions.meaning: One experiment with two outcomes, success with probability $p$ and failure with probability $1-p$.
Past failures do not change the chance of the remaining wait: $P(X>m+n\mid X>m)=P(X>n)$.

principle.text: For $n$ independent trials the chance of exactly $k$ successes counts the $\binom{n}{k}$ ways to place them, each with probability $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. The first success arriving on trial $k$ needs $k-1$ failures first.

lesson.limits: The formulas need independent trials with the same $p$ each time. Drawing without replacement from a small population breaks both conditions. Check whether a geometric count includes the successful trial: some books count only the failures before it.

example.problem: A message of 4 bits is sent, and each bit is flipped independently with probability $0.1$. What is the probability that exactly one bit is flipped?
steps: Each bit is a trial with success (flip) probability $p=0.1$, and there are $n=4$ trials, so the flip count is binomial.
One flip can sit in any of $\binom{4}{1}=4$ positions.
Each position has probability $0.1\times0.9^3=0.0729$, because one bit flips and three do not.
example.result: The probability of exactly one flip is $0.2916$.

misconceptions: Writing $p^k$ alone forgets the failures and the $\binom{n}{k}$ arrangements; exactly $k$ successes also needs the other $n-k$ trials to fail.
Treating the variance of a binomial as $np$ instead of $np(1-p)$; the mean is $np$ but the spread shrinks as $p$ moves toward 0 or 1.

recall.q: What are the mean and variance of a binomial $B(n,p)$?
recall.a: The mean is $np$ and the variance is $np(1-p)$.

recall.q: What is the probability that the first success is on trial $k$?
recall.a: $(1-p)^{k-1}p$: $k-1$ failures, then a success.

recall.q: What does memoryless mean for a geometric variable?
recall.a: After $m$ failures, the extra wait has the same distribution as at the start.

practice.stem: A fair-looking coin lands heads with probability $0.1$ and is tossed 200 times independently. Let $X$ be the number of heads. What is $\mathrm{Var}(X)$?
practice.explanation: $X$ is binomial with $n=200$ and $p=0.1$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=200\times0.1\times0.9=18$. The value $20$ tempts because it is the mean $np$; the variance carries the extra factor $1-p$.

lesson.summary: Binomial counts successes in $n$ independent trials with mean $np$ and variance $np(1-p)$; geometric waits for the first success with mean $1/p$ and no memory of past failures.

topics.title: Poisson distribution
points: Poisson(λ) counts events in a fixed interval when they occur independently at a constant average rate: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, ….
Its mean and variance are both λ, so a question that gives the average rate has given the whole distribution.
It approximates B(n, p) when n is large and p small, with λ = np.
Rescale λ with the interval: 5 calls per hour is λ = 2.5 for a 30-minute window, and the sum of independent Poissons is Poisson with the rates added.
With 4 errors per page on average, P(at most 1 error) = e⁻⁴(1 + 4) = 5e⁻⁴ ≈ 0.0916.

lesson.why: Whenever a GATE question gives an average rate of events per interval, the Poisson formulas answer it in one line.
lesson.intro: Some events arrive at random moments with a steady average rate, such as calls to a help desk or typing errors on a page. The number of events in a fixed window is then a Poisson variable. Its only parameter $\lambda$ is the average number of events expected in that window, and it fixes every probability.

definitions.meaning: The average number of events expected in the window being asked about.

principle.text: With average count $\lambda$ in the window, the chance of exactly $k$ events is given below. The mean and the variance both equal $\lambda$.

lesson.limits: It needs events that occur independently at a constant average rate. If events cluster or the rate changes over time, it does not fit. Always rescale $\lambda$ to the window in the question before using the formula.

example.problem: A server receives on average 3 requests per minute, independently. What is the probability that it receives no request in a 20-second window?
steps: The window is $20/60=1/3$ of a minute, so the average count in it is $\lambda=3\times\frac13=1$.
example.result: The probability of no request in 20 seconds is about $0.368$.

misconceptions: Using the rate per minute when the window is 20 seconds; $\lambda$ must be the average for the window asked about.
Thinking the variance is $\sqrt\lambda$ or $\lambda^2$; for a Poisson variable it equals the mean, $\lambda$.

recall.q: What do the mean and variance of a Poisson variable equal?
recall.a: Both equal $\lambda$.

recall.q: How do you adjust $\lambda$ for a window twice as long?
recall.a: Double it, because the average count grows in proportion to the window.

recall.q: How do you get $E[X^2]$ for a Poisson variable?
recall.a: Use $\mathrm{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2=\lambda+\lambda^2$.

practice.stem: Typing errors on a page follow a Poisson distribution with mean 2 errors per page. What is the probability, to four decimal places, that a page has at least one error?
practice.explanation: At least one is the complement of none: $1-P(X=0)=1-e^{-2}=1-0.1353=0.8647$. The value $0.1353$ tempts because it is $P(X=0)$, and $2e^{-2}=0.2707$ is only $P(X=1)$; neither covers every case with one or more errors.

lesson.summary: A Poisson count with average $\lambda$ in the window has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ and mean and variance both $\lambda$; rescale $\lambda$ to the window first.

topics.title: Continuous uniform distribution
points: U(a, b) has constant density 1/(b − a) on [a, b], so probability is proportional to length: P(c ≤ X ≤ d) = (d − c)/(b − a) for a ≤ c ≤ d ≤ b.
Its mean is (a + b)/2 and its variance (b − a)²/12; U(0, 1) has variance 1/12 and U(0, 4) has mean 2 and variance 4/3.
Its CDF rises linearly, F(x) = (x − a)/(b − a) on [a, b], and its median equals its mean.

lesson.why: Uniform questions reduce to measuring a length, and they test whether you can turn a condition on the variable into an interval.
lesson.intro: A continuous uniform variable takes any value in an interval $[a,b]$, and no part of the interval is favoured over another. Equal lengths are equally likely, so the chance of landing in a sub-interval is its length divided by the whole length. The density is the constant $1/(b-a)$.

principle.text: On $U(a,b)$ the probability of a sub-interval is its length over $b-a$. The mean is the midpoint, and the variance depends only on the width. The mean of a function of $X$ is the density-weighted integral of that function, not the function of the mean.
principle.tex: P(c\le X\le d)=\frac{d-c}{b-a},\quad E[X]=\frac{a+b}{2},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12},\quad E[g(X)]=\int_a^b g(x)\,\frac{1}{b-a}\,dx

lesson.limits: The length rule works only for the part of your interval that lies inside $[a,b]$; clip it first. A single point has probability 0, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. If a quantity is a nonlinear function of $X$, its mean is not the function of the mean.

example.problem: $X$ is uniform on $[2,10]$. Find $P(3\le X\le5)$, the mean, and the variance.
steps: The width is $b-a=8$, so the density is $1/8$.
The event covers length $5-3=2$, so its probability is $2/8=0.25$.

misconceptions: Using $(b-a)^2/12$ with the midpoint in it, or dividing the width by 12 without squaring; the variance uses the squared width.
Forgetting to clip: for $U(0,12)$, $P(X>3)$ uses the length $12-3$, not the length of an unbounded interval.

recall.q: What is the density of $U(a,b)$?
recall.a: The constant $1/(b-a)$ on $[a,b]$ and 0 elsewhere.

recall.q: What are the mean and variance of $U(a,b)$?
recall.a: The mean is $(a+b)/2$ and the variance is $(b-a)^2/12$.

practice.stem: $X$ is uniform on $[0,12]$. Given that $X>3$, what is the probability that $X<7$?
practice.explanation: Conditioning on $X>3$ keeps only the part of the interval where $X>3$ and rescales it to total probability 1, and the density stays constant there, so $X$ is uniform on $[3,12]$, of length 9. The favourable part is $[3,7]$, of length 4, so the answer is $4/9$. The option $1/3$ tempts because it is the unconditional $P(3<X<7)=4/12$, which ignores the condition.

lesson.summary: A uniform variable on $[a,b]$ gives probability by length ratio, with mean $(a+b)/2$ and variance $(b-a)^2/12$; clip intervals to $[a,b]$ first.

topics.title: Exponential distribution and memorylessness
points: Exp(λ) has density λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0, survival P(X > x) = e^(−λx), mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ²; a question that gives the mean has given λ = 1/mean.
It is the only continuous memoryless distribution: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t), so a component that has survived s hours is as good as new.
It models the gap between events of a Poisson process with rate λ, which is why the two distributions share the parameter.

lesson.why: Lifetime and waiting-time questions use the exponential distribution, and its memoryless property shortens many conditional problems.
lesson.intro: The exponential distribution models a waiting time, such as the time until a component fails or the gap between two arrivals. It has one parameter, the rate $\lambda$, which is the number of events per unit time. A higher rate means shorter waits, and the mean wait is $1/\lambda$.

definitions.meaning: $P(X>x)$, the chance that the wait exceeds $x$.

principle.text: The chance of waiting longer than $x$ decays exponentially, and having already waited changes nothing about the remaining wait.

lesson.limits: Memorylessness holds only for the exponential distribution (and the geometric one in discrete time). A component that wears out with age is not exponential. A question that quotes the mean has not given $\lambda$; convert with $\lambda=1/\text{mean}$.

example.problem: A component's lifetime is exponential with mean 5 hours. Find the probability that it lasts more than 3 hours, and the probability that it lasts more than 5 hours given that it has already lasted 2 hours.
steps: The mean is 5, so the rate is $\lambda=1/5=0.2$.
By memorylessness, $P(X>5\mid X>2)=P(X>3)$, the same quantity.
So the conditional answer is also $0.5488$.

misconceptions: Using the mean as the rate, so that mean 5 becomes $e^{-5x}$; the rate is the reciprocal of the mean.
Treating a used component as worse than a new one; for an exponential lifetime the survival of the extra time is the same whatever the age already reached.

recall.q: What is the survival function of $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$?
recall.a: $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$.

recall.q: What does memoryless mean here?
recall.a: $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$: time already survived does not change the remaining wait.

practice.stem: The service time at a counter is exponential with mean 4 minutes. A customer has already been served for 2 minutes. What is the probability that the service lasts more than 6 minutes in total?
practice.explanation: The rate is $1/4$. By memorylessness the extra time needed, 4 minutes, has probability $e^{-4/4}=e^{-1}\approx0.368$. The option $e^{-1.5}$ tempts because it is $P(X>6)$ without the condition; $0.632$ is the chance of stopping within the extra 4 minutes.

lesson.summary: An exponential wait with rate $\lambda$ has mean $1/\lambda$ and $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$; time already survived is forgotten, so conditional survival depends only on the extra time.

topics.title: Normal distribution, standard error and the central limit theorem
points: N(μ, σ²) is symmetric and bell-shaped about μ, with mean = median = mode = μ and variance σ²; the second parameter is the variance, not the standard deviation.
Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1), so a value 70 in a population of mean 50 and SD 10 lies 2 standard deviations above the mean.
aX + b is normal with mean aμ + b and variance a²σ², and a sum of independent normals is normal with the means and variances added.
The central limit theorem: the mean of n independent samples with mean μ and variance σ² is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n, whatever the population's shape; its standard error is σ/√n.

lesson.why: The normal distribution and the central limit theorem let you approximate averages and sums of almost anything. GATE tests recognising a normal density and reading its parameters, standardising, and standard error.
lesson.intro: A normal variable has a symmetric bell-shaped density centred at its mean $\mu$, and its spread is set by the standard deviation $\sigma$. Any normal variable can be converted to a standard one by asking how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean. For an average of many independent measurements, the average is itself nearly normal and varies less than a single measurement does.

definitions.meaning: The standard deviation of a sample mean, equal to $\sigma/\sqrt n$.
The number of standard deviations a value lies above the mean: $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$.
$\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function of $N(0,1)$, the area under the standard normal curve to the left of $z$, read from a table.

principle.text: A normal variable has density proportional to $e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, so in an exponent of the form $-(x-a)^2/b$ the mean is $a$ and $2\sigma^2=b$. Standardising turns $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ into $N(0,1)$. The central limit theorem says the mean of $n$ independent samples with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ is approximately normal for large $n$, whatever the population shape.

lesson.limits: The central limit theorem is an approximation for large $n$; it is poor for small samples from a very skewed population. The notation $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ gives the variance, so $N(50,25)$ has standard deviation 5. Samples must be independent with finite variance. For example, $e^{-x^2/18}$ has $\mu=0$ and $2\sigma^2=18$, so $\sigma=3$.

example.problem: Marks are normal with mean 60 and variance 16. Find the probability that a mark lies between 52 and 68.
steps: The area within 2 standard deviations of the mean is $\Phi(2)-\Phi(-2)=0.9545$.
example.result: The probability is about $0.954$, matching the 95 percent rule.

misconceptions: Reading the second parameter of $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ as the standard deviation; $N(60,16)$ has $\sigma=4$, not 16.
Using $\sigma/n$ or $\sigma$ itself as the spread of the sample mean; the standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

recall.q: How do you standardise a normal value $x$?
recall.a: Compute $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$, which follows $N(0,1)$.

recall.q: What is the standard error of a sample mean?
recall.a: $\sigma/\sqrt n$, where $\sigma$ is the population standard deviation.

recall.q: What does the central limit theorem say?
recall.a: For large $n$ the sample mean is approximately normal with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$.

practice.stem: A population has variance 400. The mean of a random sample of 100 independent observations is computed. What is the standard error of the sample mean?
practice.explanation: The standard deviation is $\sqrt{400}=20$, so the standard error is $20/\sqrt{100}=2$. The value $4$ tempts because it divides the variance by $n$, the value $0.2$ because it divides $\sigma$ by $n$, and $40$ would come from dividing the variance by $\sqrt n$; the correct rule divides the standard deviation by $\sqrt n$.

lesson.summary: Standardise with $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$; by the central limit theorem a mean of $n$ samples is about $N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$, with standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

topics.title: Joint distributions, covariance and correlation
points: A joint PMF p(x, y) or PDF f(x, y) gives the marginals by summing or integrating out the other variable: p_X(x) = Σ_y p(x, y).
X and Y are independent iff the joint factorises into the marginals for every x and y; one failing cell in a joint table is enough to show dependence.
Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y], and Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac·Cov(X, Y).
The correlation ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) lies in [−1, 1], with |ρ| = 1 exactly when Y is a linear function of X.
Independence implies zero covariance but not conversely: X uniform on {−1, 0, 1} and Y = X² have Cov = E[X³] − E[X]E[X²] = 0 though Y is determined by X.

lesson.why: Questions on two random variables ask for marginals, independence, covariance or correlation, and each follows from the joint table.
lesson.intro: When two random variables are studied together, their joint distribution lists the probability of every pair of values. Summing out one variable gives the marginal distribution of the other. Covariance then measures whether the two tend to be above their means together, which is positive, or on opposite sides, which is negative.

definitions.meaning: The distribution of one variable alone, found by summing or integrating the joint over the other.
The covariance scaled by both standard deviations, so it always lies in $[-1,1]$.

principle.text: Covariance is the mean of the product minus the product of the means. It scales with linear changes, and independence forces it to zero.

lesson.limits: Zero covariance does not imply independence: it detects only linear association. Independence needs the joint to equal the product of the marginals in every cell. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality keeps $\mathrm{Cov}^2\le\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)$.

example.problem: $X$ and $Y$ take values 0 or 1 with $p(0,0)=0.3$, $p(0,1)=0.2$, $p(1,0)=0.1$ and $p(1,1)=0.4$. Find $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$.
steps: The product $XY$ is nonzero only at $(1,1)$, so $E[XY]=0.4$.
example.result: $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0.1$, so the two tend to be large together; they are not independent.

misconceptions: Concluding independence from zero covariance; $X$ uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and $Y=X^2$ have covariance 0 yet $Y$ is determined by $X$.
Believing a shift changes covariance; adding constants does nothing, and only the scale factors multiply it.

recall.q: How do you get the marginal of $X$ from a joint table?
recall.a: Sum each row (or column) over the values of $Y$.

recall.q: What does $\mathrm{Cov}(aX+b,cY+d)$ equal?
recall.a: $ac\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$; the constants $b$ and $d$ drop out.

recall.q: What range can the correlation coefficient take?
recall.a: From $-1$ to $1$, with $|\rho|=1$ exactly for a linear relation.

practice.explanation: Write $3X+1$ and $-4Y+2$, so $a=3$ and $c=-4$. Then the covariance is $ac\times1.5=-12\times1.5=-18$. The value $+18$ tempts when the negative sign on $Y$ is dropped, and $-1.5$ when the constants and scales are ignored.

lesson.summary: Marginals come from summing the joint; $\mathrm{Cov}=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$ scales by $ac$ under linear maps and vanishes under independence, though the converse fails.

topics.title: Descriptive statistics: centre and spread
points: The mean is Σxᵢ/n, the median is the middle value of the sorted data (the average of the two middle values when n is even), and the mode is the most frequent value; for a frequency table the mean is Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ.
The median resists outliers and the mean does not: for 1, 2, 3, 4, 100 the mean is 22 and the median 3.
Population variance divides the squared deviations by n; sample variance divides by n − 1 to correct the bias, so for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the SDs are 2 and √(32/7) ≈ 2.14.
Spread measures: range = max − min, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, standard deviation = √variance in the data's units, and coefficient of variation = σ/μ, a unit-free ratio for comparing spreads.

A linear change y = ax + b shifts and scales the mean, median and mode to a·(value) + b, multiplies the SD and range by |a|; the CV = σ/μ becomes |a|σ/(aμ + b), so it is unchanged when b = 0 and a > 0, and with b = 0 a negative a flips its sign.

The shortcut σ² = Σx²/n − x̄² lets you merge groups or correct an entry by adjusting n, Σx and Σx²: groups of 10 with means 5 and 7, each with σ = 2, merge to mean 6 and σ² = 4 + 1 = 5, the within-group variance plus the spread of the group means.

lesson.why: Mean, median, mode and standard deviation questions appear as short numerical items, and most lost marks come from the wrong divisor or an unsorted list.
lesson.intro: A data set is a list of numbers, and two questions summarise it. Where is the middle? The mean adds the values and divides by how many there are; the median is the middle value once the list is sorted; the mode is the value that appears most often. How spread out is it? The variance averages the squared distances of the values from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, which is back in the data's own units.

definitions.meaning: The sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by $n$, used when the data is the whole group.
The same sum divided by $n-1$, used when the data is a sample drawn from a larger group.

principle.text: The mean is $\bar{x}=\sum x_i/n$. Variance sums the squared deviations and divides by $n$ for a population or $n-1$ for a sample. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

lesson.limits: The mean is pulled by extreme values, so for skewed data the median describes the centre better. A data set can have no mode or several. Use $n$ unless the question says sample variance or sample standard deviation.

example.problem: For the data 2, 3, 3, 6, 11 find the mean, the median, the mode and the sample variance.
steps: The sum is 25 and $n=5$, so the mean is $25/5=5$.
The data is already sorted and the middle (third) value is 3, so the median is 3. The value 3 appears twice and every other value once, so the mode is 3.
The deviations from 5 are $-3,-2,-2,1,6$ and their squares are $9,4,4,1,36$, which sum to 54.
The sample variance divides by $n-1=4$: $54/4=13.5$. Dividing by $n=5$ would give the population variance $10.8$.

misconceptions: Taking the middle entry of an unsorted list as the median; the data must be sorted first.
Dividing by $n-1$ when the question asks for the population variance, or the reverse; the divisor is the whole difference between $\sigma^2$ and $s^2$.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked; the standard deviation is the square root.

recall.q: How is the median found for an even number of values?
recall.a: Sort the data and average the two middle values.

recall.q: Why does the median resist outliers when the mean does not?
recall.a: The median depends only on the order of the values, while the mean uses every value's size.

recall.q: What does the sum of squared deviations get divided by for a sample?
recall.a: $n-1$, which corrects the bias that comes from measuring deviations from the sample mean.

practice.stem: For the sample 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 find the sample variance (divide by $n-1$).
practice.explanation: The mean is 6, the squared deviations are $16,4,0,4,16$ and they sum to 40. Dividing by $n-1=4$ gives $10$. The value $8$ tempts because it is the population variance ($40/5$), and $\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$ is the standard deviation, not the variance.

lesson.summary: Sort before reading the median, divide the squared deviations by $n$ for a population or $n-1$ for a sample, and take a square root to get the standard deviation.

topics.title: Median and mode of a probability distribution
points: The median m of a continuous random variable solves F(m) = 1/2, so half the probability lies on each side; for a discrete one it is the smallest m with F(m) ≥ 1/2.
The mode is where the PMF or PDF is largest; find it by differentiating the density or comparing p(k + 1)/p(k) with 1.
For Exp(λ), 1 − e^(−λm) = 1/2 gives m = ln 2/λ ≈ 0.693/λ, below the mean 1/λ, and the mode is 0: a right skew puts mode < median < mean.
For f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], F(m) = m² = 1/2 gives m = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, while the mean is 2/3 and the mode 1, the order of a left skew.
Any symmetric density, such as the normal or the uniform, has its mean and median at the centre of symmetry; the normal's mode sits there too.

For a PMF or frequency table the median is the first value whose cumulative share reaches 1/2 and the mode the most likely value; Binomial(n, p) has mode ⌊(n + 1)p⌋, two modes (n + 1)p and (n + 1)p − 1 when (n + 1)p is an integer, and Poisson(λ) has mode ⌊λ⌋, both λ and λ − 1 when λ is an integer.

lesson.why: Questions ask where a distribution splits in half or where it peaks, and the median and mode need different tools from the mean.
lesson.intro: A probability distribution has the same three centres as a data set. The mean is its balance point. The median is the point with half of the probability on each side, so the cumulative distribution function reaches one half there. The mode is the most likely value: the tallest bar of a PMF or the highest point of a density. For a lopsided distribution these three differ, and the long tail drags the mean furthest toward itself.

principle.text: The median $m$ of a continuous variable solves $F(m)=\tfrac12$. The mode of a density is where it is largest, found by differentiating, and the mode of a PMF is where $p(k+1)/p(k)$ drops below 1. For a Binomial the mode is $\lfloor (n+1)p\rfloor$.

lesson.limits: The median is in general the smallest $m$ with $F(m)\ge\tfrac12$. A discrete variable may never hit one half exactly, and a mixed one such as $\max(X,0)$ with $X$ symmetric about 0 has $F$ jump past $\tfrac12$ at a point mass, so no integration applies and the median is the atom. When $(n+1)p$ is an integer the binomial has two modes, that value and the one below. A density that is largest at the edge of its support has the mode there, and setting the derivative to zero misses it.

example.problem: A variable has density $f(x)=3x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Find its median, mode and mean.
steps: The density $3x^2$ increases on $[0,1]$, so it is largest at the right edge and the mode is 1.
example.result: Mode 1, median about $0.794$, mean $0.75$; the long tail to the left puts the mean lowest.

misconceptions: Assuming the median equals the mean; they agree only for symmetric distributions.
Finding the mode by setting $f'(x)=0$ when the density peaks at an endpoint, as $3x^2$ does at 1.
Solving $f(m)=\tfrac12$ instead of $F(m)=\tfrac12$; the median needs the cumulative probability, not the density.

recall.q: What equation defines the median of a continuous variable?
recall.a: $F(m)=\tfrac12$: half of the probability lies on each side of $m$.

recall.q: What is the mode of Binomial$(n,p)$?
recall.a: $\lfloor (n+1)p\rfloor$, with a second mode one below it when $(n+1)p$ is an integer.

recall.q: Where do the mean, median and mode sit for a symmetric single-peaked density?
recall.a: At the same point, the centre of symmetry.

practice.stem: A random variable follows Binomial$(12, 0.4)$. What is its mode?
practice.explanation: Compute $(n+1)p=13\times0.4=5.2$ and take the floor, giving 5. A direct comparison of the PMF values confirms $P(X=5)$ is the largest. The value 4.8 (the mean $np$) tempts, but it is not a possible count and the mean is not the mode; 6 comes from rounding $5.2$ the wrong way.

lesson.summary: The median solves $F(m)=\tfrac12$, the mode is the peak of the PMF or density, and a skewed distribution pulls the mean toward its long tail away from both.

topics.title: Minimum, maximum and sums of independent random variables
points: For independent X₁, …, Xₙ, P(max ≤ x) = Π P(Xᵢ ≤ x) and P(min > x) = Π P(Xᵢ > x): work with the CDF for a maximum and the survival function for a minimum.
The maximum of n independent U(0, 1) has CDF xⁿ, density nxⁿ⁻¹ and mean n/(n + 1); the minimum has mean 1/(n + 1), so E[max(X, Y)] = 2/3 for two.
The minimum of independent Exp(λ₁), …, Exp(λₙ) is Exp(λ₁ + … + λₙ): servers finishing at rates 2 and 3 per hour give a first completion after 1/5 hour on average.
For the sum of two independent random variables, add the means always and the variances only under independence; the sum of two U(0, 1) is triangular on [0, 2], not uniform.

lesson.why: Systems of parallel or racing components reduce to the minimum or maximum of independent times, and the CDF trick answers them in two lines.
lesson.intro: Suppose several independent random times run side by side, such as servers working on the same job. The maximum is the time until all have finished, and the minimum is the time until the first one finishes. Asking whether the maximum is at most $x$ is the same as asking whether every one is at most $x$, so independent chances multiply. Asking whether the minimum exceeds $x$ means every one exceeds $x$, and again they multiply.

principle.text: For independent $X_i$ with distribution functions $F_i$, the maximum is at most $x$ exactly when all are, and the minimum exceeds $x$ exactly when all do. Independent exponentials with rates $\lambda_i$ have a minimum that is exponential with the rates added.

lesson.limits: Every product above needs independence. The sum of independent variables follows a different rule: the means add always, the variances add only under independence, and the distribution is a convolution, not a product of CDFs.

example.problem: Three independent variables are each uniform on $(0,1)$. Find $P(\max\le0.8)$ and the expected maximum.
steps: The maximum is at most 0.8 only if all three are, so the probability is $0.8^3=0.512$.
In general the maximum has CDF $x^3$ and density $3x^2$, so its mean is $\int_0^1 x\cdot3x^2\,dx=3/4$.

misconceptions: Adding the CDFs instead of multiplying them; the event that all are small is an intersection of independent events.
Using the CDF for a minimum; the natural quantity is the survival function $P(X>x)$.
Taking the minimum of exponentials to have the smallest individual mean; the rates add, so it is smaller than any one mean.

recall.q: How do you find the CDF of the maximum of independent variables?
recall.a: Multiply their CDFs: $P(\max\le x)=\prod F_i(x)$.

recall.q: What is the distribution of the minimum of independent Exp$(\lambda_1)$ and Exp$(\lambda_2)$?
recall.a: Exp$(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$, with mean $1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$.

recall.q: Do variances of a sum add without any condition?
recall.a: No, only when the variables are independent, or more generally have zero covariance.

practice.stem: Three independent components fail after exponential times with rates 1, 2 and 3 per year. Find the expected time, in years to four decimal places, until the first one fails.
practice.explanation: The minimum is exponential with rate $1+2+3=6$, so its mean is $1/6\approx0.1667$. The value $1$ tempts because it is the mean of the rate-1 component alone; the first failure always comes sooner than every individual mean, and $1/3$ is the mean of the rate-3 component alone.

lesson.summary: For independent variables multiply CDFs for the maximum and survival functions for the minimum, and the minimum of exponentials is exponential with the rates added.

formulas.name: Complement rule
formulas.note: The fastest route to any “at least one” probability.

formulas.name: Inclusion–exclusion for two events
formulas.tex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
formulas.text: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
formulas.note: Use it backwards to recover P(A ∩ B) when the union is given.

formulas.name: Inclusion–exclusion for three events
formulas.tex: P(A \cup B \cup C) = \sum P(A) - \sum P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap B \cap C)
formulas.text: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣP(A) − ΣP(A ∩ B) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C)

formulas.name: Equally likely outcomes
formulas.note: Valid only when every outcome is equally likely: count ordered outcomes for dice and coins.

formulas.name: Hypergeometric probability (draws without replacement)
formulas.text: P(X = k) = C(R, k)·C(B, n − k) / C(R + B, n)
where: red and blue items in the urn
formulas.note: With replacement the draws are independent and the count is binomial instead.

formulas.name: Conditional probability
formulas.text: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), P(B) > 0

formulas.name: Multiplication rule
formulas.tex: P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)
formulas.text: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)·P(B) = P(B | A)·P(A)

formulas.name: Independence
formulas.note: Not the same as mutual exclusion, which says P(A ∩ B) = 0.

formulas.name: Total probability
where: a partition of the sample space

formulas.name: Bayes' theorem
formulas.text: P(Bᵢ | A) = P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(A | Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ)
formulas.note: The denominator is the total probability of A over every branch; leaving out a branch is the commonest slip.

formulas.name: Probability of an interval from the CDF
formulas.tex: P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
formulas.text: P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx
formulas.note: For a continuous X the endpoints carry no probability; for a discrete X they do.

formulas.name: Normalisation of a PMF or PDF
formulas.note: Solve for the unknown constant k first; every later probability depends on it.

formulas.name: Expectation of a function of X
formulas.text: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x) or ∫ g(x)f(x) dx
formulas.note: g(x) = x gives the mean, g(x) = x² gives the second moment.

formulas.name: Linearity of expectation
formulas.tex: E[aX + bY + c] = a\,E[X] + b\,E[Y] + c
formulas.text: E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c
formulas.note: Holds with no independence assumption; combined with indicators it turns counting questions into sums of probabilities.

formulas.name: Variance
formulas.note: Rearranged as E[X²] = Var(X) + (E[X])², it gives second moments in one line.

formulas.name: Variance of a linear transform
formulas.note: The shift b vanishes and the scale is squared: Var(3X + 5) = 9Var(X).

formulas.name: Variance of a sum
formulas.note: For independent X and Y the covariance is 0, so both the sum and the difference add the variances.

formulas.name: Bernoulli(p)
formulas.tex: P(X=1) = p,\; P(X=0) = 1-p,\quad E[X] = p,\; \operatorname{Var}(X) = p(1-p)

formulas.name: Binomial B(n, p)
formulas.text: P(X=k) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; E[X] = np, Var(X) = np(1 − p)

formulas.name: Geometric(p), trials to first success
formulas.note: k = 1, 2, … counts the successful trial; P(X > k) = (1 − p)ᵏ.

formulas.name: Poisson(λ)
where: average number of events in the interval asked about
formulas.note: Approximates B(n, p) with λ = np when n is large and p small.

formulas.name: Exponential Exp(λ)
formulas.tex: f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\ (x \ge 0),\quad P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x},\quad E[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda},\; \operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{\lambda^2}
formulas.text: f(x) = λe^(−λx), x ≥ 0; P(X > x) = e^(−λx); E[X] = 1/λ, Var(X) = 1/λ²
formulas.note: Check whether the question gives the rate λ or the mean 1/λ.

formulas.name: Memoryless property
formulas.tex: P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)
formulas.text: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t)
formulas.note: Exponential (continuous) and geometric (discrete) are the only memoryless distributions.

formulas.name: Standardisation (z-score)
formulas.note: Divide by σ, not σ²: N(50, 100) has σ = 10.

formulas.name: 68–95–99.7 rule
formulas.note: One tail beyond 2σ is (1 − 0.95)/2 ≈ 0.025; the exact value is 0.0228.

formulas.name: Standard error and the CLT
formulas.note: Quadrupling n halves the standard error.

formulas.name: Covariance
formulas.text: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]
formulas.note: Independent implies Cov = 0; Cov = 0 does not imply independent.

formulas.name: Correlation coefficient
formulas.note: Unchanged by shifting either variable or scaling it by a positive constant; a negative scale flips its sign.

formulas.name: Mean and variance of data
formulas.text: x̄ = Σxᵢ/n; σ² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n; s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1)
formulas.note: Use ÷n unless the question says sample variance or sample standard deviation.

formulas.name: Coefficient of variation
formulas.note: Often quoted as a percentage; it compares spread across data sets with different units or means.

formulas.name: Median of a continuous distribution
formulas.text: F(m) = ∫ f(x) dx from −∞ to m = 1/2
formulas.note: For Exp(λ) this gives m = ln 2/λ.

formulas.name: Mean and variance from a frequency table (shortcut form)
formulas.tex: \bar{x} = \frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i},\quad \sigma^2 = \frac{\sum f_i x_i^2}{\sum f_i} - \bar{x}^2
formulas.note: With every fᵢ = 1 this is σ² = Σx²/n − x̄²; keep n, Σx and Σx² to update the statistics when a value is added, removed or corrected.

formulas.name: Mean and variance of two merged groups
formulas.text: x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂); σ² = [n₁(σ₁² + d₁²) + n₂(σ₂² + d₂²)]/(n₁ + n₂)
where: x̄ᵢ − x̄, the gap between group i's mean and the combined mean
formulas.note: Averaging the two variances misses the d² terms: equal SDs of 2 around means 5 and 7 give a combined σ² of 5, not 4.

formulas.name: Mode of the binomial and Poisson distributions
formulas.note: From p(k + 1)/p(k) > 1. When (n + 1)p or λ is an integer there are two modes, that value and one less.

formulas.name: CDF of a maximum and survival of a minimum
formulas.tex: P(\max_i X_i \le x) = \prod_i F_i(x), \qquad P(\min_i X_i > x) = \prod_i \bigl(1 - F_i(x)\bigr)
formulas.text: P(max ≤ x) = Π Fᵢ(x); P(min > x) = Π (1 − Fᵢ(x))
formulas.note: Requires independence. For n iid U(0, 1): E[max] = n/(n + 1), E[min] = 1/(n + 1).

formulas.name: Minimum of independent exponentials
formulas.note: The rates add, so the expected first completion is 1/Σλᵢ, not the smallest individual mean.

problemTypes.title: Two-stage experiment: total probability, then Bayes
recipe: Name the first-stage branches (box, machine, disease status) and write their priors P(Bᵢ), checking they sum to 1.
Write the likelihood P(A | Bᵢ) of the observed outcome under each branch.
Total probability: P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
Bayes: divide the product for the branch asked about by P(A).
problemTypes.trap: Dropping a branch from the denominator, or using P(A | B) where the question asks for P(B | A).

problemTypes.title: Event algebra: conditional, union and independence checks
recipe: Recover P(A ∩ B) from whatever is given, using inclusion–exclusion if the union is given.
Compute P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A)P(B) to test independence.
Use complements and De Morgan for neither-nor events: P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).
problemTypes.trap: Calling mutually exclusive events independent; with positive probabilities they never are.

problemTypes.title: Identify the distribution, then read off a probability, mean or variance
recipe: Match the story: fixed n trials → binomial; trials until the first success → geometric; count at a rate in an interval → Poisson; waiting time at a rate → exponential.
Convert the given numbers into parameters (λ = rate × interval length, λ = 1/mean for an exponential).
Apply the PMF/PDF or the mean/variance formula, using the complement for “at least”.
problemTypes.trap: Using the rate for the wrong interval length, or the mean where the formula needs the rate.

problemTypes.title: Find the density constant, then a probability, mean or median
recipe: Integrate the density over its support and set the result to 1 to solve for k.
Probability: integrate f over the interval asked. Mean: integrate x·f(x). Median: solve F(m) = 1/2.
Sanity-check that the answer lies inside the support and that probabilities lie in [0, 1].
problemTypes.trap: Integrating over the whole real line instead of the stated support, or forgetting to multiply by k afterwards.

problemTypes.title: Expected count via indicators and linearity
recipe: Write the count as X = I₁ + … + Iₙ, one indicator per position, pair or object that might qualify.
Find P(Iᵢ = 1) for one generic indicator, using symmetry so every indicator has the same value.
E[X] = Σ P(Iᵢ = 1); no independence between indicators is needed.
problemTypes.trap: Trying to find the full distribution of X, or assuming the indicators must be independent.

problemTypes.title: Mean, median, mode and standard deviation of a data set
recipe: Sort the data first; read the median from the middle (average the two middle values for even n) and the mode from the highest count.
Compute the mean, then the squared deviations from it.
Divide by n for a population, by n − 1 for a sample, and take the square root for the SD.
problemTypes.trap: Taking the median of unsorted data, or using the wrong divisor for the variance.

problemTypes.title: Update the mean and SD after merging groups or correcting a value
recipe: Recover the sums from the given summary: Σx = n·x̄ and Σx² = n(σ² + x̄²) for a population SD.
Edit the sums: add or subtract the changed values in Σx and their squares in Σx², and adjust n for added or removed values; for two groups simply add their sums.
Recompute x̄ = Σx/n and σ² = Σx²/n − x̄², then take the square root.
problemTypes.trap: Correcting the mean but leaving the SD as given, or averaging two group variances without the spread of the group means.

problemTypes.title: Exponential memorylessness and normal standardisation
recipe: Exponential with a condition X > s: drop the elapsed s and compute P(X > t) = e^(−λt) for the remaining time.
Normal: compute z = (x − μ)/σ and use symmetry and the 68–95–99.7 rule.
Translate the tail asked about: P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.025 is half of P(|Z| > 2).
problemTypes.trap: Using σ² in place of σ when standardising, or conditioning an exponential as if it ages.

questions.stem: Box B1 contains 3 red and 2 blue balls; box B2 contains 2 red and 3 blue balls. A box is chosen with equal probability and one ball is drawn from it. The ball is red. What is the probability that it came from B1?
questions.explanation: P(R) = (1/2)(3/5) + (1/2)(2/5) = 5/10. Bayes: P(B1 | R) = (1/2)(3/5) / (5/10) = (3/10)/(5/10) = 3/5. 3/10 is the joint P(B1 ∩ R), not the conditional; 1/2 is the prior, which ignores the evidence.

questions.stem: Machines M1, M2 and M3 produce 50%, 30% and 20% of a factory's output, with defect rates 1%, 2% and 3% respectively. An item picked at random is found to be defective. What is the probability that it was made by M3? (Answer to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Total probability: P(D) = 0.5·0.01 + 0.3·0.02 + 0.2·0.03 = 0.005 + 0.006 + 0.006 = 0.017. Bayes: P(M3 | D) = 0.006/0.017 = 6/17 ≈ 0.353. M3 makes only 20% of the items but 35% of the defects because its defect rate is highest.

questions.stem: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.8. Which of the following statements are true?
options: A and B are mutually exclusive
questions.explanation: Inclusion–exclusion: P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.8 = 0.3. Then P(A | B) = 0.3/0.5 = 0.6 (true). P(A)P(B) = 0.3 = P(A ∩ B), so they are independent (true), and since P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 > 0 they are not mutually exclusive (false). By De Morgan, P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = 0.2 (true).

questions.stem: A permutation of {1, 2, …, n} is chosen uniformly at random, n ≥ 2. What is the expected number of fixed points (positions i holding the value i)?
questions.explanation: Let Iᵢ = 1 if position i holds i. P(Iᵢ = 1) = (n − 1)!/n! = 1/n. By linearity, E[Σ Iᵢ] = n·(1/n) = 1 for every n, although the indicators are dependent. Enumerating all permutations for n = 3, 5 and 6 gives an average of exactly 1. 1/n is the probability for a single position, not the expected count.

questions.stem: Typing errors occur at an average of 4 per page, following a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that a page has at most one error? (Answer to 3 decimal places.)
A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of getting exactly two sixes? (Answer to 3 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: The number of sixes is B(4, 1/6). P(X = 2) = C(4, 2)(1/6)²(5/6)² = 6 × (1/36) × (25/36) = 150/1296 ≈ 0.1157. Forgetting the C(4, 2) factor gives only one ordering, 25/1296 ≈ 0.019.

questions.stem: For which of the following random variables is the mean equal to the variance? (The geometric variable counts trials up to and including the first success.)
questions.explanation: Poisson(3): mean = variance = 3. Exp(1): mean 1/λ = 1 and variance 1/λ² = 1. Geometric(1/2): mean 1/p = 2 and variance (1 − p)/p² = 0.5/0.25 = 2. B(10, 1/2): mean np = 5 but variance np(1 − p) = 2.5; a binomial always has variance below its mean when p > 0.

questions.stem: A random variable X has density f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and 0 elsewhere. What is E[X]? (Answer to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Normalise: ∫₀³ kx² dx = k·27/3 = 9k = 1, so k = 1/9. Then E[X] = ∫₀³ x·(x²/9) dx = (1/9)·(3⁴/4) = 81/36 = 2.25. The mean lies right of the midpoint 1.5 because the density grows with x.

questions.stem: X is uniformly distributed on [0, 1]. What is Var(2X + 3)?
questions.explanation: Var(X) = (1 − 0)²/12 = 1/12. Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) = 4 × 1/12 = 1/3. 1/6 multiplies by a instead of a², and 13/12 wrongly adds the shift b = 3, which never changes a variance.

questions.stem: The lifetime of a bulb is exponentially distributed with mean 1000 hours. Given that a bulb has already worked for 500 hours, what is the probability that it works for at least 1000 more hours?
questions.explanation: λ = 1/1000 per hour. By memorylessness, P(X > 1500 | X > 500) = P(X > 1000) = e^(−1000/1000) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. Directly: e^(−1.5)/e^(−0.5) = e⁻¹. e^(−1.5) is the unconditional P(X > 1500), and 1 − e⁻¹ is the failure probability.

questions.stem: Scores are normally distributed with mean 50 and variance 100. Using the 68–95–99.7 rule, approximately what fraction of scores exceed 70?
questions.explanation: σ = √100 = 10, so z = (70 − 50)/10 = 2. About 95% lie within 2σ, leaving 5% in the two tails, 2.5% in the upper one: 0.025 (the exact value is 0.0228). 0.05 counts both tails, 0.16 is the 1σ tail, and 0.0015 is the tail beyond 3σ.

questions.stem: X takes the values −1, 0 and 1 with probability 1/3 each, and Y = X². Which statement is true?
options: Cov(X, Y) = 0 and X, Y are independent
Cov(X, Y) = 0 but X, Y are not independent
The correlation of X and Y is 1
questions.explanation: E[X] = 0, E[Y] = E[X²] = 2/3 and E[XY] = E[X³] = (−1 + 0 + 1)/3 = 0, so Cov = 0 − 0 × 2/3 = 0. Yet P(X = 0, Y = 0) = 1/3 while P(X = 0)P(Y = 0) = 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9, so they are dependent. Zero covariance rules out only linear dependence.

questions.stem: For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, treated as a whole population, which of the following are true?
questions.explanation: Sum = 40 over 8 values, so the mean is 5. The data is sorted; the middle values are the 4th and 5th, 4 and 5, so the median is 4.5, not 4. The value 4 occurs three times, so the mode is 4. Squared deviations 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 sum to 32; 32/8 = 4, so the population SD is 2. (The sample SD would be √(32/7) ≈ 2.14.)

questions.stem: Twenty observations have mean 40 and (population) standard deviation 5. It is later found that one observation recorded as 30 should have been 50. What is the corrected standard deviation? (Answer to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Recover the sums: Σx = 20·40 = 800 and Σx² = 20(5² + 40²) = 32500. Correct them: Σx = 800 − 30 + 50 = 820 and Σx² = 32500 − 900 + 2500 = 34100. Corrected mean 820/20 = 41, variance 34100/20 − 41² = 1705 − 1681 = 24, SD = √24 ≈ 4.90. Keeping the SD at 5 ignores that the bad value sat far below the mean, and plugging the new mean into the old Σx² gives 1625 − 1681 < 0, a sign the sums were not updated.

questions.stem: The service time of a request is exponentially distributed with mean 10 ms. What is its median, in ms? (Answer to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: λ = 1/10. The median m solves F(m) = 1 − e^(−m/10) = 1/2, so e^(−m/10) = 1/2 and m = 10 ln 2 ≈ 6.93 ms. It is below the mean 10 ms because the distribution has a long right tail.

questions.stem: X takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.2, 0.4. Which of the following statements are true?
options: The mean of X exceeds its median
The binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.3 has mode 3
questions.explanation: The CDF is 0.1, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0, so the smallest m with F(m) ≥ 1/2 is 3: the median is 3, not the 2.5 that averaging the two middle values suggests. The largest probability, 0.4, sits at 4, so the mode is 4. The mean is 0.1 + 0.6 + 0.6 + 1.6 = 2.9, below the median 3, so the third statement is false. For Bin(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is ⌊3.3⌋ = 3; the PMF values 0.2335, 0.2668, 0.2001 at k = 2, 3, 4 confirm the peak at 3.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent and each uniformly distributed on [0, 1]. What is E[max(X, Y)]?
questions.explanation: Let M = max(X, Y). P(M ≤ m) = P(X ≤ m)P(Y ≤ m) = m², so the density is 2m on [0, 1] and E[M] = ∫₀¹ m·2m dm = 2/3. In general the max of n iid U(0, 1) has mean n/(n + 1). 1/3 is E[min(X, Y)], and 1/2 is the mean of a single variable.

questions.stem: Two servers start jobs at the same moment. Their completion times are independent and exponential, with rates 2 per hour and 3 per hour. What is the expected time until the first of the two jobs finishes?
questions.explanation: P(min > t) = e^(−2t)·e^(−3t) = e^(−5t), so the minimum is Exp(5) with mean 1/5 hour = 12 minutes. 20 minutes is the faster server's own mean 1/3 hour, 25 minutes averages the two means (30 and 20), and 50 minutes adds them.

pitfalls.text: Mutually exclusive is not independent: events with positive probabilities that cannot occur together are strongly dependent.
Variance is not linear: Var(2X) = 4Var(X), the shift in aX + b drops out, and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) needs zero covariance.
The Bayes denominator is the total probability over every branch; leaving one out inflates the posterior.
A PMF gives P(X = x) while a CDF gives P(X ≤ x); a PDF value is a density, can exceed 1, and becomes a probability only after integration.
N(μ, σ²) is written with the variance: N(50, 100) has σ = 10, so a z-score divides by 10, not 100.
An exponential question may give the rate λ or the mean 1/λ; P(X > t) = e^(−λt) needs the rate, and memorylessness means elapsed time is ignored.
Zero covariance does not mean independence: Y = X² with X symmetric about 0 has Cov(X, Y) = 0.
Sort data before taking the median, and check whether the standard deviation divides by n (population) or n − 1 (sample).
